provenance: Generated for WORK-006. These are not collected from students or a real brainstorming session.
goal: Help first-year university students form small study groups and keep a useful weekly study habit through the semester.

notes.text: Match students taking the same course, then ask which topic they need help with so the group has a reason to meet.
Pair someone who understands a chapter with someone stuck on it; each person should also name something they want to learn.
First-year students could join by course code and exam date instead of browsing a long list of clubs.
Let me read a group's plan before joining. I don't want to commit to a study group that's only lecture recap.
At orientation, run a quick board where students find one study partner for their hardest first-semester class.
Ask each group to pick one small learning goal for next week, like finishing two practice problems.
Keep groups at four people maximum so everyone has time to ask a question.
Students from different majors might still help each other if they share a course like statistics.
Choose a recurring meeting time from everyone's weekly timetable instead of starting a new poll each week.
A short poll every Sunday could find who is free for an exam-week session.
Hold a library drop-in hour for people whose work shifts change from week to week.
Put the next meeting in calendars automatically, with an easy way to say I can't make it.
Commuters may need a 30-minute study session between lectures instead of an evening meeting.
Offer one online slot and one campus slot so travel doesn't keep someone from attending.
Show nearby study rooms with open seats before the group picks where to meet.
If two people miss a session, post one catch-up question so they can still contribute asynchronously.
Start with each person explaining one confusing step at the whiteboard.
Everyone brings two practice questions, then swaps and solves someone else's.
Use five-minute teach-backs so the group can tell whether a topic makes sense.
Keep a shared list of exam mistakes and ask a peer to explain one each week.
Begin with a short solo quiz, then compare answers and talk through disagreements.
Make flashcards together from lecture slides instead of copying one person's whole deck.
Rotate who chooses the topic so the group doesn't stay on one person's exam all semester.
End each meeting with one open question to bring to the next session.
People may show up more if they set one small weekly goal and check it off together.
A gentle reminder the morning of a session is better than chasing people after they miss it.
Pair each new member with a buddy for one check-in between group meetings.
Don't reset a shared streak when someone misses a week; ask what support would help them return.
Skip public leaderboards. Some students already feel behind, and points could make them leave.
Celebrate finishing practice problems, but don't reward raw hours spent studying.
A no-show message should let someone rejoin next week without a penalty.
Attendance may matter less than asking after a session whether people understand more.
New students may avoid asking a basic question out loud; let them submit questions anonymously.
Agree on a language everyone can follow, then write down key course terms for the group.
Post a written summary and captions so people who miss the live meeting can keep up.
Quiet members could submit a question before the session and get the first chance to discuss it.
Students with jobs need a group that can switch from live meetings to shared notes when needed.
Don't ask for exam scores during matching. Sharing grades could expose private information and scare people off.
A facilitator should make room for everyone instead of letting the fastest speaker run the session.
Could a tutor join once a month to answer questions the peer group couldn't resolve?
